items.title: baseline linerate test: first-packet latency for new flows degrades as one BESS-UPF instance serves repeated runs
items.body:
## Summary

`ptf/tests/linerate/baseline.py` (`DownlinkPerformanceBaselineTest`) passes on a freshly started UPF, but its 99.9th percentile latency check (≤ 1000 µs) fails once the same UPF instance has served a couple of earlier runs. The slow packets are a burst at the start of each run's traffic, when the test's 10,000 UE flows first reach the UPF. Steady-state latency is unaffected.

Found while validating #1331 on hardware; that PR only changes the PTF/TRex client side, so this is existing dataplane behavior.

## Environment

- Two CloudLab c220g5 hosts, Intel X710 10G (i40e, firmware 8.50), Xeon Silver 4114, Ubuntu 22.04
- BESS-UPF in DPDK mode, set up as in `scripts/docker_setup.sh`: `bess` container on two NUMA-local CPUs, 1 worker, `measure_flow: true`
- TRex v3.08 server in software mode, PTF from #1331
- Scripted setup: https://github.com/andybavier/upf-testbed (`docs/phase2.md`)

## Results

Three back-to-back runs of `baseline` after starting the UPF:

| Run | Packets ≥ 1 ms (of ~1M) | 99.9th percentile | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 125 | 60 µs | pass |
| 2 | 120 | 300 µs | pass |
| 3 | 1,178 | 2000 µs | fail |

On the long-running UPF, `baseline` failed in 3 of 4 runs, each time at 2000 µs.

## What we know

- **The tail is at the start of the traffic.** About 0.1–0.2% of packets take 1–3 ms, and 99.9% take under 50 µs. TRex's `total_max` (335 µs) leaves start-up spikes out (`CTimeHistogram`'s hot-max logic), but its histogram keeps them, and `get_latency_stats()` computes percentiles from the histogram.
- **It's a cold-flow effect.** Sending the same traffic a second time within one test, against the same installed PDRs, gave 23 packets ≥ 1 ms and a 99.9th percentile of 60 µs.
- **It isn't CPU preemption.** BESS's worker stays pinned to its CPU at 100% and is preempted about 3.6 times a second; TRex's RX and DP threads 5–20 times per run. Each costs microseconds.
- **It isn't from the test traffic generator.** TRex restarts its stream for the warm second send as well, and that send is clean.

## Suspect (not confirmed)

Per-flow state in the `FlowMeasure` modules (`preQosFlowMeasure`, `postDLQosFlowMeasure`, `postULQosFlowMeasure`). Their tables are only flipped and cleared by a session-stats read (`bess.SessionStats()`, normally from a Prometheus scrape of the PFCP agent), so on a host with no scraper they keep state between runs. The per-packet path also takes three mutexes and inserts into an `rte_hash` on each flow's first packet.

Clearing the tables between runs by scraping `/metrics` couldn't be tested cleanly. The scrape flips the buffer behind the test, and the test's own read then fails with `preQosFlowMeasure read: refusing to read active buffer (code 22)`.

## Possible next steps

- Repeat the three-run sequence with the `FlowMeasure` tables cleared between runs without flipping behind the test (for example, a read with `clear` through the same path the test uses), to confirm or rule out the suspect.
- Profile the BESS worker during the first second of a run on a UPF that has served earlier runs.
- Decide whether `baseline` should measure from a cold start, or warm the flows up first. Either way, the degradation across runs looks like a real dataplane issue.

items.title: pdrLookup has room for 16 distinct masks per UPF — how should that limit be handled?
items.body:
In [448](https://github.com/omec-project/upf/issues/448), `pdrLookup` answered ENOSPC (code 28, "failed to add a new wildcard pattern"), and the answer there was that a `WildcardMatch` table holds at most 16 distinct masks (`MAX_TUPLES`, `wildcard_match.h`), with the advice to avoid partial port masks. That reporter's log also shows the hash table's memory allocation failing, which raises the same error, so it may not have been this limit; the issue was closed by the stale bot. I would like to raise the limit itself as a question, with measurements, because it is reachable from an ordinary slice configuration rather than only from hand-built rules.

### What a mask is, in practice

`pdrLookup` is one `WildcardMatch` (`conf/up4.bess`), shared by every session on the UPF and by both directions. I parsed realistic application-filtering rules through `parsePDR` and counted masks exactly as `addPDR` builds them. A PDR's mask is set by:

- its direction (uplink and downlink PDRs differ in the tunnel and UE-address fields),
- the **prefix length** of the SDF filter's remote address,
- whether a **protocol** is given, and
- whether a **port** is given.

Nothing else changes it: not the address or port values, not TCP vs UDP, not a single port vs a short range, not which side of the flow the port is written on. Each distinct shape costs two masks, one per direction, so **eight distinct shapes fill the table** — and the default `ALLOW-ALL` rule is already one.

| Rule set | Rules | Distinct masks |
|---|---|---|
| onramp default (`ALLOW-ALL`) | 1 | 2 |
| `any`, a /24, a /16 on tcp 443, a /32 on udp 5060 | 4 | 8 |
| seven different prefix lengths plus `any` | 8 | **16 — full** |

The number of subscribers does not matter; the variety of rule shapes across all slices does. Once the table is full, any PDR needing a shape not yet present is refused, so new sessions (or modifications) for that policy fail while existing ones keep working.

### Two separate problems

1. **Slots are never released.** When a mask's last rule is deleted, its slot stays occupied (the `if (Count() == 0) { }` in `DelEntry` is empty), so the table fills with masks that are no longer in use, until pfcpiface restarts and clears it. That one is fixed by [1334](https://github.com/omec-project/upf/pull/1334): released slots are reused, and the only case that rewrites a mask under the packet path does so under a `WorkerPauser`.
2. **Sixteen is a small number for a real policy set.** Releasing slots does not help when an operator simply has more than eight rule shapes in use at once. This is what this issue is about.

### The question for (2)

Options I can see, with their costs:

- **Raise `MAX_TUPLES`.** Simple, but every occupied tuple is a hash lookup per packet batch in `LookupBulkEntry`, so the per-packet cost grows with the number of masks in use (not with the limit itself).
- **Make it a module argument**, sized by the deployment, with the same per-packet trade-off made explicit.
- **Keep 16 and make the limit visible**: document it next to application filtering, and have the configuration side reject a slice set whose rule shapes exceed it, instead of failing sessions at runtime.

Which direction would you prefer? I am happy to do the work for whichever it is.

### Related, smaller

- A port range wider than 100 ports is rejected outright (`CreatePortRangeCartesianProduct` uses the `Exact` strategy, `parse_pdr.go`), so a rule like `udp … 1024-65535` fails every session carrying it. The prefix-splitting `Ternary` strategy would accept it but spend more masks, which is presumably why it is not used. webconsole does not validate rule port ranges today.

items.title: Refactor Go control-plane architecture and reduce production language/runtime surface
items.body:
I was messing with ChatGPT and prompting it on reducing the number of components/languages needed in this project and critique the structuring. Now that agents can simply rewrite things easily, and there is a longstanding technical debt of moving BESS DSL based initialisation and routing code to Go controller. Even diagnostic UI serving as well. Ideally the python/DSL touchpoint can be entirely eliminated day-to-day, atleast in production. Probably the layers between PFCP --> BESS suggested below need not be that elaborate and can be shrunk a bit.

## Summary

The current UPF architecture has a sound high-level separation between the Go PFCP/control-plane implementation and the C++/BESS dataplane. However, the implementation has accumulated significant coupling across PFCP handling, session state, BESS-specific programming, routing, configuration, metrics, process lifecycle, Python-based BESS orchestration, and deployment concerns.

This issue proposes a staged refactor of the Go control-plane into explicit architectural layers and, in parallel, a reduction of the production runtime language surface from the current Go + C++ + Python + shell control path toward a target of:

* **Go** for all control-plane, orchestration, routing, lifecycle, configuration, reconciliation, and management logic.
* **C++** for BESS/DPDK packet processing and dataplane modules.
* **Python retained only where it adds clear value in tests**, particularly PTF/Scapy-based dataplane validation.

The intent is **not** to rewrite BESS in Go or PFCP in C++. The intent is to establish clear ownership boundaries, reduce duplicated control logic, improve failure semantics, and make the system easier to test, operate, extend, and reason about.

---

## Motivation

The repository currently presents a nominal two-layer architecture:

1. PFCP Agent in Go.
2. BESS-based dataplane.

In practice, the runtime control path is more complex.

The reference deployment currently involves multiple cooperating processes/containers:

* Go `pfcpiface`
* C++ `bessd`
* Python `route_control.py`
* Python `bessctl http`
* shell-based lifecycle/bootstrap operations
* Python-based `.bess` pipeline construction

This creates a distributed control plane inside a single pod/process namespace.

Configuration and dataplane state are consequently managed by several different components and languages. The same UPF configuration is consumed by both Go and Python, BESS is manipulated through both Go gRPC clients and Python `pybess`, and lifecycle/state transitions are spread across application code, `.bess` scripts, shell hooks, and Kubernetes configuration.

The resulting complexity is larger than the source-language count alone suggests.

The main architectural problem is therefore not simply "too many languages". It is:

> Multiple languages and processes currently participate in the same control-plane responsibility.

The desired end-state should follow a stronger ownership rule:

> **Go owns control and desired state. C++ owns packet processing.**

---

## Current architectural issues

### 1. The datapath abstraction exists but is not a strong boundary

There is a `datapath` interface, which is directionally correct, but the current abstraction leaks application and PFCP-oriented concepts into the datapath boundary.

The interface currently includes responsibilities such as:

* datapath lifecycle
* rule mutation
* connectivity
* UPF initialization
* slice programming
* end-marker handling
* metrics access

The principal mutation API is effectively of the form:

```go
SendMsgToUPF(
    method upfMsgType,
    allRules PacketForwardingRules,
    newRules PacketForwardingRules,
) uint8
```

This API exposes an operation-oriented mutation model rather than a semantic desired-state contract.

The PFCP application is therefore still tightly coupled to how datapath changes are programmed.

Additionally, construction currently hard-wires BESS as the implementation rather than injecting a datapath implementation:

```go
pfcpIface.fp = &bess{}
```

This means the advertised datapath plugin boundary is compile-time and structural rather than a clean dependency boundary.

### 2. BESS-specific behavior is spread too widely

The Go BESS integration currently carries a large number of responsibilities:

* gRPC connection management
* PDR programming
* FAR programming
* QER programming
* notification sockets
* end-marker handling
* QoS state
* metrics
* datapath lifecycle
* failure handling
* batch programming

The BESS implementation has consequently become a large central component rather than a narrow adapter behind a stable domain interface.

A stronger architecture should ensure that BESS protobufs, module names, command names, gate numbers, and gRPC details are contained entirely within a BESS adapter package.

### 3. PFCP transport, session orchestration, and datapath programming are too tightly coupled

`PFCPConn` currently owns or participates in:

* UDP transport
* PFCP sequence handling
* heartbeats
* pending requests
* association lifecycle
* session storage
* UPF access
* request handling
* shutdown behavior

This makes it difficult to isolate:

* PFCP protocol behavior
* session state transitions
* datapath programming
* failure semantics

PFCP handlers should translate protocol requests into domain operations rather than directly coordinating implementation-level datapath details.

### 4. Session state is not modeled as desired vs applied state

The system currently programs BESS incrementally and then derives PFCP responses from the result.

A particularly important correctness issue exists around batch programming timeout behavior.

If a BESS batch times out, the datapath state may be partially applied. The current implementation can return PFCP success because returning failure could cause the control plane to forget about a partially-installed session.

That is an understandable defensive behavior, but it exposes an architectural gap:

> The application cannot reliably determine whether desired session state equals applied datapath state.

A timeout is not equivalent to success or failure. It is an **unknown outcome**.

This should eventually be represented explicitly and reconciled.

### 5. Constructors perform significant runtime side effects

Object construction currently performs operations such as:

* interface and address resolution
* datapath initialization
* timer setup
* IP pool setup
* connection/setup behavior

Some lower-level code also terminates the process via fatal logging.

Constructors should construct objects. Lifecycle methods should perform I/O and runtime initialization.

Lower-level packages should return errors rather than deciding that the process must terminate.

### 6. Session storage is in-memory and tied closely to PFCP connection lifecycle

The current session store abstraction is useful, but the default implementation is an in-memory `sync.Map`.

The broader model currently lacks a strong concept of:

* desired session state
* applied datapath generation
* reconciliation after partial failure
* process restart recovery
* datapath restart recovery

BESS startup also clears state, further emphasizing that the system currently depends on destructive reinitialization rather than convergence toward desired state.

### 7. Configuration has multiple owners

Go contains a typed UPF configuration model and validation logic.

Python pipeline/orchestration code also consumes the same `upf.jsonc` configuration and interprets fields independently.

This creates two configuration ownership domains:

```text
upf.jsonc
   ├── Go interpretation
   └── Python interpretation
```

Schema evolution therefore requires coordination across languages and implementations.

The JSONC parser in Go is also based on comment stripping rather than a full JSONC parser, which is an avoidable source of parsing edge cases.

### 8. Routing control is implemented in Python but fits naturally into the Go control plane

`route_control.py` currently performs significant production control-plane work:

* Linux route monitoring
* neighbor monitoring
* route cache management
* neighbor cache management
* unresolved ARP handling
* BESS module creation/deletion
* BESS route updates
* retry behavior
* datapath pause/resume behavior

This is not merely scripting glue.

It is core UPF control-plane behavior.

The same functionality can be implemented naturally in Go using:

* Linux netlink/rtnetlink libraries
* the existing generated Go BESS gRPC client
* the same application lifecycle and metrics infrastructure as PFCP

This is the highest-value production Python component to migrate first.

### 9. The BESS pipeline itself is configured through Python-based `.bess` code

`up4.bess` currently performs substantial production configuration:

* worker setup
* port creation
* interface discovery
* parser construction
* PDR lookup graph creation
* FAR graph creation
* QER/QoS graph construction
* GTP-U encap/decap
* flow measurement
* routing modules
* NAT-related setup
* Unix socket notification modules
* end-marker handling

This pipeline is expressed using the Python-based BESS DSL.

However, the BESS gRPC API already exposes the primitives required to construct the graph programmatically:

* `CreateModule`
* `DestroyModule`
* `ConnectModules`
* `DisconnectModules`
* `ModuleCommand`
* worker management
* port management
* traffic-class management
* reset operations

The Go control process can therefore eventually own BESS pipeline construction directly.

### 10. The runtime architecture behaves like a distributed monolith

The current reference pod combines several tightly coupled processes that share:

* configuration
* lifecycle
* process namespace
* sockets
* BESS control API
* shell startup coordination

The deployment is operationally more complex than the conceptual architecture.

The target should be closer to:

```text
                PFCP
                  │
                  ▼
          ┌───────────────────┐
          │    Go UPF Agent   │
          │                   │
          │ PFCP              │
          │ Sessions          │
          │ Routing           │
          │ Reconciliation    │
          │ Pipeline control  │
          │ Metrics / HTTP    │
          └────────┬──────────┘
                   │
              gRPC / Proto
                   │
                   ▼
          ┌───────────────────┐
          │      bessd        │
          │   BESS + DPDK     │
          │ UPF datapath mods │
          └───────────────────┘
```

Two production processes and two implementation languages.

---

# Proposed Go architecture

The Go control plane should be restructured around explicit responsibilities and one-way dependency flow.

Suggested target structure:

```text
cmd/
  upf/
    main.go

internal/
  app/
    app.go
    lifecycle.go

  config/
    config.go
    load.go
    validate.go

  pfcp/
    server.go
    peer.go
    connection.go
    heartbeat.go
    handler_association.go
    handler_session.go
    parser.go
    response.go

  session/
    model.go
    service.go
    compiler.go
    store.go
    memory_store.go

  datapath/
    interface.go
    model.go

    bess/
      adapter.go
      client.go
      pipeline.go
      pdr.go
      far.go
      qer.go
      route.go
      notify.go
      stats.go

  routing/
    manager.go
    source.go
    netlink_linux.go
    neighbor.go

  ipam/
    pool.go

  tunnel/
    fteid.go

  telemetry/
    prometheus.go
    http.go

  logging/
    logger.go

test/
  integration/
```

The exact package names are less important than the dependency rule:

```text
PFCP transport
      │
      ▼
Session service
      │
      ▼
Domain datapath model
      │
      ▼
BESS adapter
      │
      ▼
BESS protobuf / gRPC
```

BESS implementation details must not flow upward.

---

# Architectural rule

The refactor should follow this rule:

> **Protocol packages translate. Domain services decide. Adapters perform I/O. `main` wires dependencies together.**

Concretely:

```text
PFCP request
    │
    ▼
PFCP parser
    │
    ▼
Session command
    │
    ▼
Session service
    │
    ▼
Session compiler
    │
    ▼
Datapath SessionProgram
    │
    ▼
BESS adapter
    │
    ▼
BESS protobuf/gRPC
```

The control plane should avoid direct:

```text
PFCP → BESS
```

translation.

---

# 1. Introduce a datapath domain model

The datapath API should consume semantic desired-state objects rather than PFCP-oriented mutation requests.

Example:

```go
package datapath

type SessionID uint64
type PDRID uint32
type FARID uint32
type QERID uint32

type SessionProgram struct {
    ID   SessionID
    PDRs []PDR
    FARs []FAR
    QERs []QER
}

type PDR struct {
    ID         PDRID
    Precedence uint32
    Match      Match
    FAR        FARID
    QERs       []QERID
}

type FAR struct {
    ID     FARID
    Action ForwardingAction
}

type QER struct {
    ID       QERID
    Uplink   Rate
    Downlink Rate
    QFI      uint8
}
```

PFCP code should compile incoming PFCP structures into this model.

The BESS adapter should compile this model into BESS protobuf/module operations.

This gives us two stable translation boundaries:

```text
3GPP/PFCP → UPF domain

UPF domain → BESS
```

---

# 2. Replace `SendMsgToUPF` with semantic APIs

The datapath interface should not expose low-level operation selectors such as `upfMsgType`.

Proposed initial interface:

```go
type Datapath interface {
    ApplySession(
        ctx context.Context,
        program SessionProgram,
    ) (ApplyResult, error)

    DeleteSession(
        ctx context.Context,
        id SessionID,
    ) error

    ApplySlice(
        ctx context.Context,
        slice SliceProgram,
    ) error

    Stats(
        ctx context.Context,
    ) (Stats, error)

    Close() error
}
```

The application should say:

```go
result, err := datapath.ApplySession(ctx, desired)
```

rather than:

```go
datapath.SendMsgToUPF(
    upfMsgTypeMod,
    oldRules,
    newRules,
)
```

As reconciliation matures, this may evolve into an even more declarative contract:

```go
Reconcile(
    ctx context.Context,
    desired DesiredState,
) (ReconcileResult, error)
```

That does not need to be introduced in the first refactor.

---

# 3. Separate datapath programming, telemetry, and lifecycle interfaces

The current datapath abstraction contains unrelated concerns.

Prefer smaller interfaces where useful:

```go
type SessionProgrammer interface {
    ApplySession(
        context.Context,
        SessionProgram,
    ) (ApplyResult, error)

    DeleteSession(
        context.Context,
        SessionID,
    ) error
}

type TelemetryReader interface {
    Stats(context.Context) (Stats, error)
}

type Lifecycle interface {
    Start(context.Context) error
    Close() error
}
```

Application components should depend only on the interface they actually require.

This prevents routing, telemetry, and PFCP code from depending on a large god-interface.

---

# 4. Introduce a central `SessionService`

Session orchestration should move into a dedicated domain service.

Example:

```go
type SessionService struct {
    store    Store
    compiler Compiler
    datapath datapath.SessionProgrammer
    ipam     IPAllocator
    fteids   FTEIDAllocator
}
```

Suggested API:

```go
func (s *SessionService) Create(
    ctx context.Context,
    req CreateRequest,
) (Session, error)

func (s *SessionService) Modify(
    ctx context.Context,
    req ModifyRequest,
) (Session, error)

func (s *SessionService) Delete(
    ctx context.Context,
    id SessionID,
) error
```

The service should own transaction ordering.

For example, session creation:

```text
parse PFCP request
      │
      ▼
validate
      │
      ▼
allocate resources
      │
      ▼
compile SessionProgram
      │
      ▼
program datapath
      │
      ▼
commit session state
      │
      ▼
return success
```

Failure handling should explicitly release any resources allocated before commit.

PFCP handlers should not directly coordinate these steps.

---

# 5. Separate PFCP transport from domain behavior

The PFCP package should be split conceptually into:

```text
pfcp/
  server.go
      UDP listener and dispatch

  peer.go
      association transport state

  heartbeat.go
      PFCP heartbeat behavior

  handlers.go
      request → domain operation

  parser.go
      PFCP IE → domain command

  response.go
      domain result → PFCP response
```

A session-establishment handler should conceptually become:

```go
func (h *Handler) HandleSessionEstablishment(
    ctx context.Context,
    req *message.SessionEstablishmentRequest,
) (*message.SessionEstablishmentResponse, error) {

    command, err := h.parser.ParseEstablishment(req)
    if err != nil {
        return h.responses.RejectEstablishment(err), nil
    }

    result, err := h.sessions.Create(ctx, command)
    if err != nil {
        return h.responses.RejectEstablishment(err), nil
    }

    return h.responses.Establishment(result), nil
}
```

The PFCP package should not know:

* BESS module names
* BESS protobuf types
* BESS gate numbers
* BESS command names

---

# 6. Make the BESS implementation a strict adapter

All BESS-specific implementation should live under:

```text
internal/datapath/bess
```

Only this package should import generated BESS protobuf packages.

Suggested internal split:

```text
bess/
  client.go
      gRPC connection
      timeouts
      retries

  adapter.go
      implementation of datapath interfaces

  pdr.go
      domain PDR → BESS commands

  far.go
      domain FAR → BESS commands

  qer.go
      domain QER → BESS commands

  batch.go
      batch programming semantics

  pipeline.go
      initial BESS pipeline construction

  route.go
      route/neighbor programming

  notify.go
      downlink/report notifications

  stats.go
      datapath statistics
```

The package boundary should explicitly prevent imports such as:

```text
pfcp     → bess_pb
session  → bess_pb
routing  → bess_pb
config   → bess_pb
```

The allowed dependency is:

```text
datapath/bess → bess_pb
```

---

# 7. Model datapath outcomes correctly

Datapath programming must distinguish:

* operation definitely applied
* operation definitely rejected
* outcome unknown

Suggested representation:

```go
type ApplyStatus uint8

const (
    ApplyStatusApplied ApplyStatus = iota + 1
    ApplyStatusRejected
    ApplyStatusUnknown
)

type ApplyResult struct {
    Status     ApplyStatus
    Generation uint64
}
```

A gRPC deadline should not automatically become either "success" or "failure".

If BESS may have partially applied a mutation, the result is unknown and should eventually trigger reconciliation.

---

# 8. Introduce desired vs applied state

Sessions should eventually distinguish control-plane intent from confirmed datapath state.

Example:

```go
type Session struct {
    ID SessionID

    Desired SessionProgram
    Applied SessionProgram

    Generation        uint64
    AppliedGeneration uint64

    State State
}
```

Suggested lifecycle:

```go
type State uint8

const (
    StatePending State = iota
    StateActive
    StateUpdating
    StateDeleting
    StateFailed
)
```

This enables a later reconciliation loop:

```text
desired generation = 42
applied generation = 41
          │
          ▼
reconciler detects drift
          │
          ▼
apply generation 42
```

This does not require persistent storage in the first phase, but the model should not prevent persistence later.

---

# 9. Keep the session store interface but make semantics explicit

A cleaner store API would look like:

```go
type Store interface {
    Get(
        context.Context,
        SessionID,
    ) (*Session, error)

    Put(
        context.Context,
        *Session,
    ) error

    Delete(
        context.Context,
        SessionID,
    ) error

    List(
        context.Context,
    ) ([]Session, error)
}
```

For the in-memory implementation, prefer explicit synchronization:

```go
type MemoryStore struct {
    mu       sync.RWMutex
    sessions map[SessionID]*Session
}
```

over `sync.Map` unless measurement shows that `sync.Map` materially improves performance.

Explicit locking will make future multi-step consistency rules easier to implement and review.

---

# 10. Move `route_control.py` into Go

The route-control process should be migrated into:

```text
internal/routing
```

Suggested conceptual split:

```go
type Source interface {
    Events(context.Context) (<-chan Event, error)
}

type RouteDatapath interface {
    UpsertRoute(
        context.Context,
        Route,
    ) error

    DeleteRoute(
        context.Context,
        Route,
    ) error

    UpsertNeighbor(
        context.Context,
        Neighbor,
    ) error

    DeleteNeighbor(
        context.Context,
        Neighbor,
    ) error
}
```

and:

```go
type Manager struct {
    source   Source
    datapath RouteDatapath
}
```

The Linux implementation can use rtnetlink/netlink.

The BESS implementation of `RouteDatapath` remains in:

```text
internal/datapath/bess
```

This lets route behavior be tested independently from BESS.

Migrating this component removes one production Python sidecar and consolidates datapath ownership under the Go process.

---

# 11. Move BESS pipeline construction into Go

Once route control is migrated, the next production Python dependency to remove should be `.bess` pipeline construction.

Introduce a typed pipeline model:

```go
type PipelineSpec struct {
    Workers []WorkerSpec
    Ports   []PortSpec
    Modules []ModuleSpec
    Links   []LinkSpec
}
```

For example:

```go
func BuildUPFPipeline(
    cfg config.Config,
) PipelineSpec
```

and:

```go
func ApplyPipeline(
    ctx context.Context,
    client *Client,
    spec PipelineSpec,
) error
```

The implementation can use the existing BESS gRPC API for:

* workers
* ports
* modules
* module connections
* module commands
* resets

The migration should be protected by golden tests comparing:

* module types
* module arguments
* gates
* links
* worker assignments
* expected port configuration

between the existing `.bess` pipeline and the new Go-generated specification.

Once complete, production no longer needs:

```text
bessctl run up4
```

for pipeline construction.

---

# 12. Remove the Python `bessctl http` sidecar from the default runtime

The production deployment currently starts a separate BESS HTTP process.

The default production architecture should not require a Python sidecar purely for datapath inspection.

Options:

1. expose the required diagnostic information through the Go management HTTP server;
2. retain BESS web tooling only in a debug/development image;
3. make the BESS HTTP sidecar explicitly optional.

This should not block the more important route-control and pipeline migrations.

---

# 13. Use one composition root

Dependency construction should happen in one place: `cmd/upf/main.go`.

`main.go` should be intentionally boring.

Conceptually:

```go
func main() {
    cfg := config.MustLoad(...)

    log := logging.New(cfg.Log)

    bessClient := bess.NewClient(cfg.Datapath)

    dp := bess.NewDatapath(
        bessClient,
        bess.Config{...},
    )

    store := session.NewMemoryStore()

    sessions := session.NewService(
        store,
        dp,
        ipam.New(...),
        tunnel.NewFTEIDAllocator(...),
    )

    pfcpServer := pfcp.NewServer(
        cfg.PFCP,
        sessions,
    )

    routeManager := routing.NewManager(
        routing.NewNetlinkSource(),
        dp,
    )

    app := app.New(
        pfcpServer,
        routeManager,
        telemetry.New(...),
        dp,
    )

    if err := app.Run(context.Background()); err != nil {
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}
```

No dependency-injection framework is needed.

Plain Go constructors are sufficient.

---

# 14. Constructors must not perform runtime I/O

Adopt the rule:

```text
New(...)
    constructs

Start(ctx)
    performs runtime initialization

Close()
    releases resources
```

Avoid constructors that:

* open sockets
* connect to BESS
* clear datapath state
* start goroutines
* resolve runtime state
* terminate the process

Example:

```go
dp := bess.New(cfg)

if err := dp.Start(ctx); err != nil {
    return err
}
```

This is substantially easier to test than constructors that perform hidden side effects.

---

# 15. Lower-level packages must return errors, not terminate the process

Library/internal packages should never call `Fatal`, `Fatalln`, or `os.Exit`.

Use:

```text
internal package
      │
      ▼
return error
      │
      ▼
application decides policy
      │
      ▼
main logs termination
```

This is essential for:

* deterministic tests
* graceful cleanup
* recoverable startup behavior
* reusable components
* proper error context

---

# 16. Standardize lifecycle using `context.Context`

Every operation crossing an I/O or lifecycle boundary should accept a context.

Examples:

```go
ApplySession(
    context.Context,
    SessionProgram,
)

Run(
    context.Context,
) error

Stats(
    context.Context,
) (Stats, error)
```

Timeouts should be applied at policy boundaries:

```go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(
    ctx,
    cfg.Datapath.ProgramTimeout,
)
defer cancel()
```

instead of relying on package-global timeout variables.

---

# 17. Centralize process lifecycle with `errgroup`

Application startup/shutdown should be owned by the application layer rather than distributed across components.

Example:

```go
func (a *App) Run(ctx context.Context) error {
    g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)

    g.Go(func() error {
        return a.pfcp.Run(ctx)
    })

    g.Go(func() error {
        return a.routes.Run(ctx)
    })

    g.Go(func() error {
        return a.http.Run(ctx)
    })

    err := g.Wait()

    return errors.Join(
        err,
        a.datapath.Close(),
    )
}
```

`main` should translate OS signals into context cancellation.

---

# 18. Centralize configuration ownership in Go

The Go process should become the sole production owner of UPF configuration semantics.

Recommended configuration structure:

```go
type Config struct {
    PFCP      PFCPConfig
    Datapath  DatapathConfig
    Routing   RoutingConfig
    Telemetry TelemetryConfig
}
```

Where practical, new networking configuration should use `net/netip` rather than `net.IP`.

Once Python no longer owns route or pipeline behavior, Python should no longer need to interpret `upf.jsonc`.

At that point we should also consider replacing the current JSONC comment-stripping implementation with either:

* a real JSONC parser;
* plain JSON;
* YAML, if comments are considered important.

Configuration format migration should be treated separately from architectural migration.

---

# 19. Use typed domain enums instead of implementation constants

Datapath-independent values should be modeled explicitly:

```go
type Direction uint8

const (
    Uplink Direction = iota + 1
    Downlink
)
```

Likewise for:

* forwarding actions
* interface roles
* session state
* gate state
* datapath result state

BESS-specific numeric conversions belong exclusively in the BESS adapter.

Avoid propagating conventions such as:

```text
0 = N3
1 = N6
2 = N9
```

through domain code.

---

# 20. Strengthen tests around architectural boundaries

Testing should be aligned with the proposed layers.

Suggested layout:

```text
internal/session/
  compiler_test.go
  service_test.go

internal/pfcp/
  handler_test.go
  association_test.go

internal/datapath/bess/
  translation_test.go
  adapter_test.go
  pipeline_test.go

internal/routing/
  manager_test.go

test/integration/
  pfcp_bess_test.go
```

The existing fake BESS implementation should become a deliberate test adapter.

Important test boundaries:

### PFCP → domain

Golden tests should verify:

```text
PFCP Session Establishment Request
              │
              ▼
expected Session command / SessionProgram
```

### Domain → BESS

Separate tests should verify:

```text
SessionProgram
      │
      ▼
expected BESS protobuf/module operations
```

### Pipeline equivalence

During `.bess` migration:

```text
existing up4.bess topology
          vs
Go PipelineSpec
```

should be compared for semantic equivalence.

This prevents one refactor from simultaneously changing:

* PFCP behavior
* session semantics
* BESS translation

without detection.

---

# Proposed migration sequence

This work should be staged so that architectural cleanup and language reduction do not become one high-risk rewrite.

## Phase 1 — Establish package boundaries

* Introduce `internal/session`.
* Introduce `internal/datapath`.
* Move BESS implementation to `internal/datapath/bess`.
* Constructor-inject the datapath instead of hard-wiring `&bess{}`.
* Split BESS protobuf types from domain code.
* Preserve current runtime behavior.

**Goal:** architectural separation with minimal functional change.

---

## Phase 2 — Introduce `SessionProgram`

* Define a datapath-independent session model.
* Introduce PFCP → domain/session compiler.
* Introduce domain → BESS translators.
* Replace direct use of `PacketForwardingRules` at the datapath boundary.
* Add golden tests for translation.

**Goal:** eliminate direct PFCP-to-BESS coupling.

---

## Phase 3 — Replace `SendMsgToUPF`

* Introduce `ApplySession`.
* Introduce `DeleteSession`.
* Introduce typed `ApplyResult`.
* Represent unknown datapath outcomes explicitly.
* Remove `upfMsgType` from the public datapath contract.

**Goal:** semantic datapath API.

---

## Phase 4 — Clean lifecycle and error handling

* Remove fatal exits from internal packages.
* Make constructors side-effect free where practical.
* Introduce explicit `Start`/`Close`.
* Propagate `context.Context`.
* Centralize goroutine ownership using `errgroup`.

**Goal:** predictable startup/shutdown and testability.

---

## Phase 5 — Introduce desired/applied state

* Add session generation.
* Track desired vs applied program.
* Represent `ApplyStatusUnknown`.
* Add basic reconciliation hooks.
* Preserve in-memory storage initially.

**Goal:** correct behavior under partial datapath failure.

---

## Phase 6 — Port route control from Python to Go

* Add Linux route/netlink source.
* Add route and neighbor domain types.
* Implement BESS route adapter.
* Port cache/retry behavior from `route_control.py`.
* Run both implementations in comparison/testing mode if useful.
* Remove route-control Python container when parity is established.

**Goal:** remove Python from runtime routing control.

---

## Phase 7 — Port BESS pipeline construction to Go

* Define `PipelineSpec`.
* Implement BESS pipeline builder.
* Create topology equivalence tests against `up4.bess`.
* Move workers/ports/modules/links into Go-managed startup.
* Remove `bessctl run up4` from the production startup path.

**Goal:** make Go the sole production datapath-control owner.

---

## Phase 8 — Simplify deployment

Target production pod/process topology:

```text
container/process 1:
    Go upf-agent

container/process 2:
    bessd
```

Optional debug tooling may remain separate.

Remove default production dependence on:

* `route_control.py`
* `.bess` execution
* Python `bessctl http`
* shell-based BESS orchestration where equivalent Go lifecycle exists

**Goal:** Go + C++ production runtime.

---

## Phase 9 — Revisit repository boundaries

Once the control plane is cleanly separated from BESS internals, consider whether the full BESS source tree should remain vendored in the UPF application repository.

Possible future model:

```text
UPF repo
    Go control plane
    UPF-specific schemas/config
    integration tests

BESS repo/artifact
    C++ dataplane framework
    DPDK
    native modules
```

UPF CI would consume an immutable BESS version/image/artifact.

This would significantly reduce the number of toolchains required for ordinary UPF development.

This phase is optional and should happen only after interfaces are stable.

---

# Non-goals

This issue does **not** propose:

* rewriting BESS or DPDK in Go;
* rewriting the PFCP agent in C++;
* removing C++ from the dataplane;
* converting PTF/Scapy tests to Go immediately;
* introducing Rust or another implementation language;
* replacing protobuf/gRPC solely for language-reduction purposes;
* performing the entire migration in one pull request.

Python is still appropriate for specialized test tooling where it materially improves developer productivity.

The initial language-reduction target is specifically the **production control path**.

---

# Expected end-state

The final production architecture should have clear ownership:

## Go

Owns:

* PFCP transport
* PFCP associations
* heartbeats
* PFCP parsing/response generation
* session state
* session compilation
* IP allocation
* F-TEID allocation
* route monitoring
* neighbor monitoring
* BESS pipeline construction
* BESS control operations
* datapath desired state
* reconciliation
* metrics
* HTTP management
* process lifecycle
* configuration validation

## C++

Owns:

* BESS runtime
* DPDK
* packet parsing
* GTP-U fast path
* PDR lookup execution
* FAR execution
* QER enforcement
* QoS dataplane behavior
* packet measurement
* dataplane-native UPF modules

## Python

Retained primarily for:

* PTF
* Scapy-based packet tests
* specialized development/test utilities where justified

Python should not be required for normal production UPF operation.

---

# Acceptance criteria

This issue can be considered complete when the following architectural properties hold:

* [ ] BESS is constructor-injected rather than instantiated directly by the PFCP application.
* [ ] PFCP/session packages do not import BESS protobuf packages.
* [ ] Routing code does not import BESS protobuf packages.
* [ ] BESS-specific logic is isolated under a dedicated adapter package.
* [ ] The datapath interface no longer exposes `SendMsgToUPF(method, ...)`.
* [ ] Session programming uses a datapath-independent `SessionProgram` or equivalent model.
* [ ] PFCP handlers call a session-domain service rather than programming BESS directly.
* [ ] Lower-level packages return errors rather than terminating the process.
* [ ] Long-running components use `context.Context` for cancellation.
* [ ] Application lifecycle is coordinated from one composition root.
* [ ] Datapath programming distinguishes applied/rejected/unknown outcomes.
* [ ] Desired vs applied session state can be represented.
* [ ] Route control runs in Go rather than the Python sidecar.
* [ ] Production BESS pipeline construction can be performed from Go.
* [ ] `bessctl run up4` is no longer required in the default production startup path.
* [ ] Python BESS HTTP tooling is optional rather than a required production container.
* [ ] The reference deployment can run with Go + C++ as the only production implementation languages.
* [ ] Existing PTF and integration tests continue to validate dataplane behavior.

---

# Suggested intermediate PR breakdown

To keep reviewable changes small, the implementation could be split approximately as follows:

1. Move BESS code behind `internal/datapath/bess`; add dependency injection.
2. Introduce datapath domain types.
3. Add PFCP/session compiler layer.
4. Replace `SendMsgToUPF` with semantic session APIs.
5. Split `PFCPConn` responsibilities.
6. Introduce `SessionService`.
7. Clean constructors, error handling, and lifecycle.
8. Add desired/applied generation model.
9. Port route control to Go.
10. Introduce `PipelineSpec`.
11. Port `up4.bess` pipeline generation to Go.
12. Remove Python route/pipeline sidecars from Kubernetes deployment.
13. Make BESS web/debug tooling optional.
14. Reassess BESS repository/build ownership.

Each PR should preserve behavior unless the PR explicitly targets a correctness issue.

---

# Risks

## Datapath behavior regressions

The `.bess` pipeline contains substantial topology and module configuration logic. A direct rewrite without equivalence testing could introduce subtle forwarding changes.

Mitigation:

* golden topology tests;
* packet-level PTF regression tests;
* temporary side-by-side pipeline specification comparison.

## Route-control parity

`route_control.py` contains retries, route caching, neighbor handling, ARP behavior, pause/resume semantics, and BESS module manipulation.

Mitigation:

* port behavior incrementally;
* create event-driven unit tests;
* replay netlink event traces where possible;
* retain Python version during validation.

## Session semantic changes

Moving from incremental mutations to desired-state programming may reveal assumptions currently hidden in the BESS adapter.

Mitigation:

* introduce the new model while preserving existing command ordering initially;
* separate architectural migration from atomicity/reconciliation improvements.

## Scope

This is a multi-phase architecture initiative rather than a single refactor.

Mitigation:

* maintain explicit phases;
* keep each PR behaviorally narrow;
* avoid combining package moves with unrelated dataplane changes.

---

# Additional cleanup that can follow

Several smaller issues can be addressed once the major architecture is in place:

* rename `cmd/pfcpiface` to something such as `cmd/upf` or `cmd/upf-agent`, since the process will own substantially more than a PFCP interface;
* clean up the historical Go module name if compatibility permits;
* replace fragile JSONC comment stripping;
* review the initial PFCP UDP receive buffer sizing;
* minimize runtime packages in the BESS image;
* separate test/build Python dependencies from production runtime dependencies;
* reduce generated Python protobuf bindings once production Python control components are removed.

These should not distract from the larger layering work.

---

# Design principle

The primary design objective should not be "use one language".

It should be:

> **One language owns each architectural concern.**

For this repository, the cleanest division is:

```text
Go:
    control, orchestration, desired state, lifecycle

C++:
    packet processing

Python:
    tests and specialized development tooling
```

That preserves the performance strengths of BESS/DPDK while substantially reducing operational and cognitive complexity in the UPF control stack.

items.title: How to improve the performance of two-way(uplink/downlink) transmission ?
items.body:
I'm facing an issue when testing the performance of UFP :
Performance of one way(UL or DL) is about 2M pps,
but two way(UL and DL) is still 2M pps, not as expected 4M pps.
(Using two DPDK bound NICs for N3 an N6.)

Really appreciate if any further suggestion.  
Thank you in advance !

****
I tried to make the performance of two-way touch 4M pps, but these are not workable :
 (1) Pinning multiple cores
 (2) 2 worker threads 

**(1) Pinning multiple cores :**
  Isolate 4 cores on the same NUMA node, but only one core is 100% loading.

  - At host (/etc/default/grub) :  
         GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="isolcpus=2,4,6,8"

  - In script(docker_setup.sh) :  
         # Run bessd
         docker run --name bess -td --restart unless-stopped \
	--cpuset-cpus="2,4,6,8"  --cpus 4 \
                   ...

  After running docker_setup.sh and no UL/DL data,  command "htop" : 100% loading is only one core, not four cores.


**(2) 2 worker threads :**
  There is error when executing docker_setup.sh, if workers=2.

  - In conf/upf.json :
    "": "Number of worker threads. Default: use 1 thread to run both (uplink/downlink) pipelines",
    "workers": 2,

  - Executing docker_setup.sh : 
    Error and stop.

  - Error log :  ([P.S.]  enp3s0f0 : N3 NIC  /  enp3s0f1 : N6 NIC  )
